paragraphs: Abba Arikha is Rav. (1) Rav’s name was Abba; just as Rabbi Yehudah Hanasi is called “Rabbi” in the Land of Israel, so he is called “Rav” in Babylonia (Rashbam, chapter Chezkat Habattim, 52a). Rashbam explains likewise in chapter Arvei Pesachim, 119b. In Yevamot 57b Shmuel says, “And Abba concedes to me.” Rashi explains that this is an expression of esteem: being older than Shmuel, he was called Abba, like “my prince” or “my master.” End quotation. In Berakhot 47a Shmuel says, “If young pigeons were brought to Abba, would he not eat them?” Rashi explains that he called him Abba out of respect; likewise in Chullin 38, beginning of a. In Shabbat 53a Shmuel says, “If Abba said this, he knows nothing of the laws of Shabbat.” Rashi explains, “Abba, my colleague,” as in avrekh, a father to the king; similarly Rashi in Ta'anit 4, end of b. In Berakhot 60b Rashi offers no explanation. In Eruvin 94, beginning of a, Shmuel says, “If Abba objects”; in Pesachim 80a Rashi offers no explanation. In Chullin 45b Shmuel says, “If Abba said this, he knows nothing of tereifot.” Rashi explains: “Shmuel calls him this because Rav was greater than he. I have heard ‘Abba,’ and some read ‘Abba, my colleague.’” End quotation. This implies that this was the Gemara’s reading, meaning the chief of colleagues, that is, of all the sages (so Rashal writes). In Arvei Pesachim 107a Rav Huna says to him, “Has Abba begun earning coins from beer?” In Bava Kamma 11a Shmuel says, “Abba concedes to me”; Rashi: Rav. In the Jerusalem Talmud, Bava Kamma, chapter 1, halakhah 1: “And Abba concedes to me. Who is Abba? Rabbi.” Its commentator writes that it should read “Rav.” Bava Kamma 62a: “And Abba does not know”; likewise in chapter Chalon, 78a. Tosafot, Yevamot 57b, reject Rashi’s explanation of Abba as an honorific and follow the Arukh, entries Abba and Abaye: this was his name, as in Berakhot 47 and chapter Haro'eh, 62a: “Rav Kahana said, ‘Abba’s mouth looks as if he had not tasted food.’” But how could Rav Kahana, Rav’s student, call him by name? In Chelek 100 he said that Gehazi was punished for this. (The wording “said” implies that Rav Kahana said it, but our reading is, “Rabbi Yochanan said: Why was he punished?”) Perhaps Rav Kahana was Rav’s student-colleague, as in Sanhedrin 36, beginning of b: he needed Rav’s received teaching but not his reasoning. End of Tosafot. In Chullin 38a Tosafot likewise follow the Arukh: Abba was his name, and Shmuel, his colleague, used his name; likewise in Arvei Pesachim and the Eruvin passage, “If Abba objects.” In chapter Reshit Hagez, 137b, Rabbi Yochanan asked Issi bar Hini, “Who heads the academy in Babylonia?” He answered, “Abba Arikha.” (Rashi: he was tall in his generation, as in chapter Hamappelet, 24, end of b; see below, Abba Shaul.) He said, “I remember sitting seventeen rows behind Rav before Rabbi: sparks of fire went from Rabbi’s mouth to Rav’s mouth, and we did not know what they were saying—and you call him Abba Arikha!” (Rashi: when he was here, before descending to Babylonia, he was more important than I; he sat before Rabbi, while I sat seventeen rows behind him.) This expressly implies that Abba is not an honorific. Yet he would not have been angry merely for using his name, but for calling him Arikha, an uncomplimentary expression; Rabbi Yochanan himself called him Abba, Chullin 84, end of a: “Abba is from a family of healthy people.” But there is a difficulty concerning Rav Hamnuna (it should read Rav Huna): Yoma 87, end of a, “Rav Huna said: Abba is going to kill a person.” He was his student, yet called him by name. (Rashi explains: “Abba, his master,” since Rav Huna was Rav’s student. Tosafot Yeshanim ask how Rav Huna, his full student, could use his name, and answer that perhaps he called him Abba respectfully, as “my father.” End quotation.) Rashi’s view that Abba was an honorific resolves this. End of Tosafot. In Pesachim 40a Rav Nachman calls Rabbah Abba; Rashi: an expression of mastery. In Beitzah 29b Rav Nachman says concerning Rava bar Huna Zuti, “Abba”; Rashi: my colleague (see there). These support Rashi’s explanation, since their names were not Abba. Rav read in the priest’s place (Megillah 22a).

(2) His father was Ivo (see there). He descended from Shimi, brother of King David (see Rabbi Chiyya). Rabbi Chiyya and Rav sat at a meal before Rabbi; Rabbi Chiyya called Rav bar pachatei (Berakhot 13b, 43a, 46, end of b). In Shabbat 3, beginning of b, and 29a Rashi explains “son of great men.” The Arukh explains “son of a prince,” from “governors and deputies”; some say bar pa'atei, as in “he shall crush the corners of Moab.” His wife distressed him; his son Chiyya (see there) would reverse his father’s instructions (Yevamot 63a). He had a son Ivo (see there), and Rav Chanan was his son-in-law. Rabbana Ukva and Rabbana Nechemyah were his daughter’s sons (see there).

(3) (a) He was the student of Rabbi Chiyya his uncle, brother of his father Ivo. (Rav calls Rabbi Chiyya chavivi, Eruvin 12, end of b, and Makkot 11a. Rashi: he was brother to his father and his mother. The Arukh: “my dear and beloved,” or a contraction of the Aramaic for “uncle, his father’s brother.”) Rabbi Chiyya said to Rabbi, “My sister’s son is going down to Babylonia: may he issue rulings and judge?” (He did not, however, authorize him to permit firstborn animals; see Sanhedrin 5a for the reason.) He called him “my sister’s son” on account of his wisdom: “Say to wisdom, You are my sister.” In truth he was both his brother’s son and his sister’s son (Sanhedrin 5; Pesachim 4; Mo'ed Katan 20, end of a). Since he was both, why did Rabbi Chiyya say to Rabbi “my sister’s son is going down to Babylonia”? Surely on account of his wisdom. When Rabbi Chiyya was under Rabbi’s censure, he taught Rav all the principles of the Torah (see below, Chiyya). In Chullin 16a Rav sat behind Rabbi Chiyya, who sat before Rabbi. Rav asked Rabbi Chiyya what Rabbi had said. He replied, “A vav written on a log,” meaning an unsound reason. Jerusalem Talmud, Ma'aser Sheni, chapter Kerem Reva'i, halakhah 8: Rav had flax that was damaged and asked Rabbi Chiyya whether to slaughter a bird and mix the seed to remedy it. There, at ע"ב, it writes that Rav was Rabbi Meir’s student. (See below, Rabbi Chiyya: the flax incident happened to Rabbi Chiyya, who asked Rabbi.) Not having seen when Rabbi accepted the yoke of Heaven, he asked Rabbi Chiyya, Berakhot 13b; see there. Rav said, “I found in Rabbi Chiyya’s secret scroll that Issi ben Yehudah said,” Shabbat 6b, 96b; Bava Metzia 92a. Rav said in Rabbi Chiyya’s name, Shabbat 92, end of a; 98a; 99a; 138, end of a. (b) Eruvin 13: Rav said, “My sharpness beyond my colleagues comes from seeing Rabbi Meir from behind.” (Rashi: when I studied before him, I sat in the row behind him.) Likewise Rashbam, Chezkat Habattim 51b. Rav also speaks in Rabbi Meir’s name in Chullin 63b, chapter Haro'eh 60, end of b, and 61a, and Pesachim 3b. Some read, “Rabbi said: My sharpness,” etc.; Tosafot, Menachot 104, beginning of a. (c) Rav was Rabbi’s student, Beitzah 22b. He said, “I was in Rabbi’s voting assembly, and they began the count with me,” Gittin 59, beginning of a; Sanhedrin 36. Rabbi asked Rav, Horayot 11, beginning of b. Rav attended Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya while seated; Rabbi Yochanan attended while standing (chapter Ellu Tereifot; see above what I brought from Reshit Hagez). (d) Maimonides, introduction to the Mishneh Torah, writes that Rav received teaching from Rabbi Yannai. (Raavad objects: “This never was and never came into being.”) Yuchasin writes that Maimonides has support in Yevamot 93a: Rav Huna follows Rav, Rav follows Rabbi Yannai, and Rabbi Yannai follows Rabbi Chiyya. Rashi explains: Rav Huna follows Rav, meaning he received it from his master Rav, and so each from the master above him. End quotation. (The new Talmud editions read, “He was of this one’s generation.”) But chapter Kirah, 39, end of b, requires examination: Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Yannai’s name, in Rav’s name. This suggests the reverse, that Rav was Rabbi Yannai’s teacher. In my view this is why She'erit Yosef counted Rabbi Yannai among Rav’s students. Yet I think it a scribal error: it should read, “Rabbi Yannai said in Rabbi’s name” (see there). (e) Sh.H.K., 32b, writes that Rav and Shmuel received from Rabbi Chanina bar Chama (see there: it is false), in year 3999 (this is incorrect: he descended to Babylonia in 3979), and died in 4003.

(4) Rav is a tanna and may disagree: Chullin 122b; Bava Batra 42a; Eruvin 50, end of b; Gittin 38b. The Arukh, entry Rav, first entry, writes: “Rav is a tanna and disagrees.” Rav Hai Gaon explains: “From the precise language of the masters we found Rav Abba in three places: Berakhot 49a, ‘Rav Abba said: One must give thanks at the beginning and end’; Ketubbot 81, end of a, ‘Rav Abba said: I asked Sumchos’; and Shabbat 135b, ‘Rav Abba said: She immersed and then gave birth.’ Abba is Rav, as I explained under Abaye. Another explanation of ‘Rav is a tanna and disagrees’: Rav is among Levi, bar Kappara, Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi, and Rabban Gamliel son of Rabbi, who are tannaim; he is also among amoraim such as Shmuel, the first Rav Huna, and others. A baraita does not displace his words, because he is a tanna disagreeing with a tanna.” End quotation. Under Abaye the Arukh writes: “Some tannaim are called Rav in particular places: ‘Rav Chama said’ in Shabbat; ‘Rav Abba said’ concerning thanks at beginning and end in Berakhot; ‘Rav Abba said: I asked Sumchos’ in Ketubbot.” End quotation. Yuchasin writes: “What the Gaon says in Shabbat, chapter Rabbi Eliezer, ‘Rav Abba said: She immersed,’ etc., I have not found in the Gemara, Rashi, or Tosafot as Abba, but as Rav Chama.” (So too the Arukh under Abaye above apparently had Rav Chama.) “I found in another Tosefta, Chullin, chapter 6: ‘Rabbi Abba said: This is one of the things that Rabbi Chiyya said had no answer; Rabbi Eliezer answered,’ etc. Likewise Tosefta, Beitzah, first chapter: ‘Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Eliezer Hakappar, answered.’ In the Gemara, Chullin 84b–85a: ‘This is one of the things that Rabbi Chiyya said, I have no answer; Rabbi Elazar Hakappar Berabbi gave an answer.’” Rashi and Tosafot, Beitzah 9a, on the difficulty from Rav against Rav Chanan: although Rav is an amora, an objection is raised from him (see below, Shmuel), because he was the teacher of all the diaspora in that generation, apart from Shmuel. End quotation. Maharik writes likewise. See Keritot, Leshon Limmudim, gate 3, section 141: “Rabbi Chiyya is a tanna and disagrees,” Bava Metzia 5a, and likewise Rav and Rabbi Yochanan. Plainly they are not tannaim, since they are not mentioned in the Mishnah; rather, they have the standing of tannaim and can disagree with a mishnah or baraita, etc. For us they count as tannaim, but Rav did not regard Rabbi Yochanan as a tanna, nor did Rabbi Yochanan regard Rav as a tanna, etc. Tosafot, Ketubbot 8, end of a, likewise: Rav is a tanna, but Rabbi Yochanan did not hold him to be a tanna. This is not said of Rabbi Yochanan: Tosafot, Yevamot 7b; Niddah 23b; likewise the commentator to Tamid, beginning of chapter 1.

(5) His colleague was Shmuel. Rashbam and Tosafot, Arvei Pesachim 103, beginning of a: Rav, Levi, and Shmuel were colleagues. Shmuel told him that if he would not eat the oil permitted by Rabbi Yehudah Nesia, “I will write against you as a rebellious elder”; he pressed him, and he ate (see there). Rav Sherira Gaon writes, as cited in Yuchasin: “In Rabbi’s days Rav descended to Babylonia” (he was in the Land of Israel and came to Babylonia, Rashi, Ta'anit 10a), “in year 530” (it should be 531) “of the era of documents, which is year 3979 from creation. Rabbi Shila (see there) was head among the rabbis after Rabbi and was called head of the academy in Babylonia. Rav came to Rabbi Shila’s place and stood as his interpreter.” (Yoma 20b: they did not recognize him. Rav rendered keri'at gever as a man’s call; Rabbi Shila told him to say a rooster. Rav answered, “A flute for free men,” etc. He asked, “Are you Rav, accustomed to interpreting before Rabbi Chiyya? Sit in your honor; I am unworthy of having you as interpreter”; see there.) “When Rav Shila died, Rav and Shmuel were there. Rav would not become head over Shmuel, nor would Shmuel, because Rav was much older. As in Bava Kamma 80a: Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Assi came to a circumcision celebration—some say a redemption of a son. Rav did not enter before Shmuel; Shmuel did not enter before Rav [Assi]; Rabbi Assi did not enter before Rav. They said, ‘Who shall stay outside?’, etc. Therefore Rav left Shmuel in Nehardea, his home” (likewise Rashi, Ta'anit 21b), “a place of Torah, and went away to a place without Torah: Sura, which is Mata Mechasya. Many Jews lived there, yet they did not even know what was forbidden or permitted. Rav said, ‘I will settle here’” (he was head of the academy in Sura: Rashi there, Gittin 6a, Chullin 45b), “‘so that Torah will exist here,’ as Chullin 110a explains: Rav found an open field and fenced it.” (See Eruvin in several places, 6a, 100b.) “When he came to Tatlafush, he taught them and ruled for them concerning the prohibition of udders. Rav acquired his academy’s garden by a tzurta (a drawing or figure); it had been a convert’s property” (see Bava Batra 54a). “He gathered students, spread much Torah, and established a court there. There were two great courts in Babylonia: the earlier one in Nehardea, and the one Rav established in Sura. Hence Shmuel said: We write a prosbul only in the court of Sura or Nehardea, etc. Rav and Shmuel would occasionally meet. He headed Sura for twenty-four years and died in 4003.” End quotation. (See part I, year 3979.) Charta of Argiz was Rav’s locality (see below, Rav Hamnuna). When the rabbis departed from Rav’s academy, twelve hundred rabbis remained as guests at his table (chapter Shenei Dayyanei Gezerot). Rav said, “I did not become wealthy until I saw turnip tops in their beds in a dream” (Berakhot 57b). When he came to Darshish he announced, “Who will be mine for a day?” (Yoma 18b; Yevamot 37b). “Our masters in Babylonia” means Rav and Shmuel (Sanhedrin 17). He was called “the great court” (Kiddushin, chapter Ha'omer). Rabbi Yochanan wrote to him, “Before our master in Babylonia” (Chullin 95b). Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan are kera'ei: their words are like Scripture; another explanation: lords (see Shmuel). He cursed Shmuel, and Shmuel had no surviving male children throughout Rav’s life (see there). He prayed with Shmuel in the Shaf Veyativ synagogue in Nehardea (Rosh Hashanah 24b). Shmuel applied to Rav, “No iniquity will befall the righteous,” chapter Ellu Tereifot 59a; Niddah 65a; Yevamot 121 (see Rav Shila and Binyamin Genuvya). Rav Kahana asked Rav, “If zealots did not strike him, what is the law?” Rav forgot his received teaching on it and could not answer. In a dream they recited to Rav Kahana, “Judah has dealt treacherously,” etc. He told Rav what they had recited, and Rav recalled his teaching: “Judah has dealt treacherously,” etc. (chapter Hannisrafin, 82, beginning of a). She'erit Yosef, 35a, writes that Rav studied with Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi (see there) and Rabbi Malkiyo (see there: he erred). Rav, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Chaviva taught: throughout the order Mo'ed, whenever this group occurs together, some amoraim replace Rabbi Yochanan with Rabbi Yonatan (Rashi, Shabbat 54: all four together; Rashi, Sukkah 4, end of b). Megillah 7a; Tosafot, Shabbat 54b, explain “taught” as referring to the following statement. The Talmud then interrupts to say that throughout Mo'ed this group replaces Rabbi Yochanan, etc.; “taught” does not refer to the substitution. He said, “A person should never absent himself from the study hall even for one hour. Levi and I were before Rabbi when he said this teaching: in the evening he said one thing, in the morning another. I, being in the study hall, retracted; Levi, being absent, did not” (Beitzah 24b). He said, “Beside this pillar Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yose prayed the Shabbat prayer on Friday” (Berakhot 27b). Rabbah bar bar Chana gave him money to buy land, and he bought it for himself (Kiddushin 59a). Jerusalem Talmud, Pe'ah, chapter Beit Shammai, halakhah 3: when Rav descended to Babylonia he said, “I am like Ben Azzai.” An elder came and asked about people found slain one atop the other; he answered, etc., and asked Rabbi, etc. See Sedeh Yehoshua there: a similar account occurs in the Babylonian Talmud, chapter Eglah Arufah, where Abaye says, “I am like Ben Azzai,” etc., and someone asks about two slain people. He writes that these were two incidents. Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah, chapter 1, halakhah 7: Rav, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yonatan, bar Kappara, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. In chapter Ellu Tereifot Resh Lakish says of him, “May that man be remembered for good.” An official named Adrakan loved him as Antoninus loved Rabbi. When the official died, Rav said, “The bond has come apart” (Avodah Zarah 10b). He loved Rabbi Chanina bar Shilat as a father loves a son (see there).

(6) (a) Sifra and Sifrei have been attributed to Rav (see Maimonides’ introduction to Zera'im; B.Tz.L.; Abarbanel’s introduction to Nachalat Avot; and Shevilei Emunah, path 8). The introduction to Middot Aharon writes: “I think they learned this from Berakhot 18b: ‘He struck the lion on a snowy day’—he studied Sifra of Rav’s academy on a winter’s day.” (Rashi: Torat Kohanim.) Rashi, Ellu Tereifot 66, beginning of a, did not think so: he writes that a baraita taught in Torat Kohanim is called “the tanna of Rav’s academy”; it is called Sifra of Rav’s academy because it was familiar to all his academy’s students. From his words in Gittin 67 he seems to hold that Rabbi Akiva composed it: he cites Avot deRabbi Natan, etc., “He made coins: he arranged the midrash Sifra and Sifrei separately and taught them separately to his students,” etc. In chapter Hannechenakin: anonymous Mishnah is Rabbi Meir; anonymous Tosefta is Rabbi Nechemyah; anonymous Sifra is Rabbi Yishmael (see below, Rabbi Akiva). Some sages wished to infer that Rabbi Yishmael was its author. In my view they erred: “anonymous Sifra is Rabbi Yishmael” must be understood as “anonymous Mishnah is Rabbi Meir”—Rabbi, who arranged the mishnayot, stated an anonymous mishnah according to Rabbi Meir; so too the author of Sifra stated an anonymous baraita according to Rabbi Yishmael, who said it according to Rabbi Akiva. End quotation. See Techillat Chokhmah 32b: Sifra of Rav’s academy means Torat Kohanim; the other books of Rav’s academy run from “They shall send out of the camp” to the end of the book. End quotation. See Rashbam, chapter 2, 124b, at length. Rashi, Yoma 74a, explains: the books Vayedabber and Elleh Haddevarim. (b) B.Tz.L.: Rav composed it according to Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai, and composed Mekhilta (see Rabbi Oshaya). (c) Tosafot, Sanhedrin 17b: anonymous “they say in Rav’s academy” is in Rav’s name; in chapter Hasho'el, Bava Metzia, and chapter Beit Kor, they object to Rav from “they say in Rav’s academy.” See Asheri, chapter Kirah, and Techillat Chokhmah, gate 3, chapter 2, section 142: “they say in Rav’s academy” is Rav himself. Halikhot Olam writes that it is not Rav himself but the academy; likewise Techillat Chokhmah, gate 3, chapter 1, section 30. (d) Sh.L., letter vav: wherever the Talmud says “But the master said,” it means Rav. End quotation. Also cited in a gloss to Maimonides’ introduction to Zera'im.

(7) He practiced ten acts of piety: (a) He did not look beyond four cubits (see below, Shimi). (b) He did not walk with his head uncovered. (c) He observed three meals. (d) He directed his heart in prayer. (e) He did not look to the sides. (f) He went around so as not to trouble the public. (g) He did not eat at an optional feast (chapter Gid Hanasheh, 95b). In a gloss to Yuchasin, letter resh, it writes: “This is incumbent on every Torah scholar. Rather, it appears to be what is in Midrash Eikhah on ‘He ground my teeth with gravel’ (and the Jerusalem Talmud, end of Ta'anit): after eating all the world’s delicacies, Rav would eat earth to fulfill this verse. I proposed the mnemonic, ‘Take out a lip and bring in a latter lip.’” End quotation. At first glance he appears to have understood Rav as doing this throughout the year after eating, rather than only on the eve of the ninth of Av; otherwise it would hardly deserve counting as special piety. But Magen Avraham, Orach Chayyim 552, writes that he did it on the eve of the ninth of Av. Beit Yosef there, citing Nachmanides’ Torat Ha'adam and Hagahot Maimuniyyot, attributes it to Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai, not Rav. Yet I saw in Rokeach, section 310: “In Eikhah: Rabbi, when eating the ninth-of-Av meal, would take a piece of bread and dip it in earth, etc.; and likewise Rav in the Jerusalem Talmud.” End quotation. (h) Whoever offended him, he would go to appease him. Yoma 87, end of a: a butcher offended him; twelve months passed without his coming. On the eve of Yom Kippur he still did not come, so Rav said, “I will go appease him.” Rav Huna met him and asked where he was going. “To appease so-and-so.” He said, “Abba is going to kill a man.” He went and called at the door. The man said, “Go away” (the reading of Ein Yaakov; the Gemara reads, “Are you Abba?”), “I have nothing to do with you.” He was splitting a head; an axe slipped, struck his head, and killed him. Chiddushei Aggadot writes that the butcher was punished for offending Rav without appeasing him and for calling him Abba by name. End quotation. This follows the Gemara’s reading, where the butcher calls him Abba. Although Rashi explains Abba as an honorific, the butcher should still have addressed him as “my master”; this is easily understood. Further there: Rav was expounding a portion before Rabbi. Rabbi Chiyya entered, and he returned to the beginning; bar Kappara entered, and he returned to the beginning; likewise Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi, etc. Rabbi Chanina bar Chama entered; Rav said, “Must we return to the beginning for everyone who comes?” Rabbi Chanina took offense. Rav went to him on twelve eves of Yom Kippur, but he was not appeased. The Gemara objects that one need not ask more than three times, and answers: Rav was different (he was stringent with himself—Rashi). How could Rabbi Chanina act so, when one who overlooks offenses has all his sins overlooked? Rather, he dreamed of Rav being raised on a palm tree; one raised on a palm tree becomes head. He said, “I will drive him away, and we shall not be driven away.” (Rashi: Rabbi Chanina was academy head; fearing that he would die because one reign cannot encroach on another, he would drive Rav to Babylonia to become head there, so he would not die on his account. Bach: when Rav became academy head, public needs would burden him and prevent study; see Orach Chayyim 606.) (i) His voice was pleasant, and he stood to interpret. (j) He was regular in tzitzit and tefillin. Maimonides, Laws of Dispositions, chapter 2, writes that Rav, our holy master’s student, never engaged in idle conversation. Kesef Mishneh there says: “I found this in chapter Hayashen about Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai; for Rav I do not presently know the source.” End quotation. Responsa Mekom Shmuel, end of section 65: plainly it is Chagigah 5b, “‘He tells a person what his speech was’—Rav said: even excessive conversation between a man and his wife,” etc. He wonders why Kesef Mishneh did not say that Rabbi Eliezer never spoke idle talk, mentioned in Hayashen before Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai. This is no difficulty: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai preceded his student Rabbi Eliezer in generation. Jerusalem Talmud, Nedarim, chapter 10, halakhah written here as וג': a person came before him to litigate with a wealthy man. In the arrogance of his wealth, the rich man refused; Rav cursed him. Immediately a royal decree confiscated all his possessions. He came to Rav to pray for him; Rav did so and they were restored. He was fastidious: even after washing his hands he ate with a cloth (Chullin 107b). Also at the end of chapter Hakometz. When he went out to judge he said, “Of his own will he goes out to death,” etc. (Yoma 86, end of b).

(8) Rav lived long enough to see his grandson Shimi, son of his son Chiyya (see there). K.N.Y., part 3, end of section 63, writes: Rav is the Rabbi Abba mentioned in the Zohar; he lived four hundred years. Another K.N.Y. has the reading “one hundred years”; he was Rabbi Chiyya’s teacher in this wisdom and afterward attended Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya. On an old manuscript leaf: Rav lived three hundred years. The matter is puzzling: if he lived so long, why is there no mention of him in the time of the earlier tannaim? (At the end of Yonat Elem: whenever it says “Rav was silent” [Sukkah 7, beginning of a; Bava Metzia 97, beginning of a], he could have answered according to the esoteric teaching—being Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai’s outstanding student among the masters of secrets—but did not wish to reveal it. “Rabbi Abbahu” there is a scribal error; it should read “Rabbi Abba.” Responsa Chavvot Yair, section 132, writes: although I questioned this from the discussion in Beitzah 6, end of a, as to why he was silent, that means he should also have answered according to the revealed teaching. Thus Bava Kamma 11a, “From his silence, that is not the law,” is no difficulty. One may also answer that indeed we do not decide laws by secrets, for in several places we do not rule like Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. Sanhedrin, chapter Arba Mitot: “Both shall die,” etc.—Rav was silent. Tosafot, Bava Batra 62a: Rav was sometimes silent because he did not care to answer, and sometimes because he conceded. Asheri, chapter Hamokher et Habbayit 61: Rav was silent because he did not care to answer them. Rav Sheshet’s remark about Rav, “When Rav was drowsy and lying down he said this teaching,” is not derogatory but great praise; see there at length. In Zohar, Bereshit [see above], Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai called his son and Rabbi Abba “Peniel.”)

(9) When he died, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna decreed that for a whole year they should not bring myrtle and palm branches with music before bridegrooms. One person breached the restriction and a snake bit him (see there). When Rabbi Yochanan was told that Rav had died, he tore thirteen garments and said, “The man whom I feared has gone” (see there). Shmuel tore twelve garments (see there). Rav Adda bar Ahavah attended his burial and tore his garment (see there). They took earth from Rav’s grave for a one-day fever. When told, Shmuel said they had acted properly, since land cannot become prohibited (Sanhedrin 47b). His grave is eighteen cubits long (G.A.Y.). Arioch king of Ellasar was reincarnated in him (see Shmuel). His soul was reincarnated in Rashi (see above, part I, year 4865).

(10) (a) In a dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan, the law follows Rabbi Yochanan (see there), apart from three cases, Beitzah 4a. Responsa Chavvot Yair writes: this is surprising, for Rabbi Yochanan wrote to him “Before our master,” and Rav is a tanna, whereas this is not said of Rabbi Yochanan, as above; see there. (b) Between Rav and Rabbi Chanina, the law follows Rav (Keritot, Yemot Olam, gate 3, section 21). (c) Between Rav and Levi, the law follows Rav: Levi was subordinate to Rabbi Chanina, as chapter Hannose, 103, shows, so if Rav prevails against Rabbi Chanina, all the more against Levi. (See below, Levi, where it appears he was not subordinate.) See responsa Ralbach, section 11; Tosafot, Bava Metzia, chapter Hazahav, concerning acquisition with the buyer’s utensil, likewise. Responsa H.K., part 2, section 103, at 101, writes: Rif and Rosh rule like Rav because Rav follows the first tanna and Levi follows Rabbi Yehudah, and because the discussion’s conclusion follows Rav. When ruling like Rav Nachman against Rav Sheshet that acquisition cannot be made with fruit, they say, first, the law follows Rav Nachman in civil matters and Rav Sheshet in prohibitions, and second, the conclusion follows Rav Nachman. Their not writing for Rav and Levi, “The law follows Rav, and furthermore,” etc., implies that they did not find the rule clear. Tosafot say that the wording “to exclude Levi” implies the law follows Rav, and Rav Nachman in chapter Hashole'ach holds like Rav. They do not give Rif and Rosh’s reason that Rav follows the first tanna. One may therefore doubt whether Tosafot generally hold that between Rav and Levi the law follows Levi, so that even if Rav follows the first tanna, Levi prevails—as, according to most decisors, Rava prevails even if Abaye follows the first tanna and Rava follows Rabbi Yehudah. Beit Yosef, Orach Chayyim 560, concerning bridegrooms’ crowns, rules like Levi against Rav; see Maggid Mishneh. (d) Between Rav Huna and Rav, the law follows Rav (Halikhot Olam, gate 2, chapter 2, 35a; Keritot, gate 3, at section 21). This is plain, since Rav Huna was Rav’s student. (e) The law follows Rav in prohibitions, Bekhorot 49, beginning of b, except for that case there. Rashi, Pesachim 76, beginning of a: although we follow Rav in prohibitions, here we follow Shmuel because two baraitot support him. Tosafot, chapter Ein Tzadin, 29, beginning of b: some rule like Shmuel here although the law follows Rav in prohibitions. On this rule see Asheri, Bava Kamma, chapter 4; Tosafot, Eruvin 43a, 77b, and end of Kol Gaggot; Mo'ed Katan 8b; Niddah 24b. (f) Shabbat 22a: Abaye said, “In everything my master”—Rabbah—“acted like Rav, except three.” There, 40a, and Arvei Pesachim 101a: it means Rav’s stringencies, and not where he was refuted. Tosafot, Eruvin 93b: in eruvin and mourning we follow the lenient view even against Rav. Eruvin 90b: Rav and Shmuel disagreed and Shmuel himself said the law follows Rav (see Shmuel). (g) Where Rav and Shmuel disagree on something involving both prohibitions and monetary matters, whom to follow requires examination. (h) Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Haro'eh: Rav says one must say “You”; Shmuel says one need not. Does the rule that Rav prevails in prohibitions apply also to the Jerusalem Talmud? This requires examination (responsa H.K., part 2, at 103). Responsa Chavvot Yair writes: in doubt I think we should follow Rav, since in any case he was greater than Shmuel (Bava Kamma 80b; Chullin 95b); moreover, not everyone agrees that Shmuel prevails in civil matters. See Zevachim 38b; Chullin 52b; Niddah 24b; Tosafot, Kiddushin 23b; Ran, opening of Nedarim on a partial declaration for consecration; also chapter 11 at 88b; the last responsum in Maharit; Tosafot Yom Tov, Berakhot 8:4; Shevuot 43b. See Beit Yosef, Choshen Mishpat, end of section 67, on Rav Sheshet’s dispute: the monetary law of remission is termed a prohibition. End quotation. (i) The rule that Rav prevails in prohibitions concerns Shmuel alone; here Rabbi Yochanan, whom we follow against Rav, stands with Shmuel (Tosafot, Shabbat 53a). Tosafot, Kiddushin 79b, s.v. Vehilkheta Kerav: despite this general rule, an express ruling for Rav was necessary because some amoraim rule like Shmuel.
